messages.content: I want to develop streaming speech recognition that handles temporarily ambiguous speech accurately, but once it commits a word, that word must stay fixed. The goal is to keep word error rate within 5% relative of an equally trained revisable streaming baseline, keep 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds, and make zero revisions after commitment.

That sets a joint accuracy, latency, and finality goal. The system must recognize speech as it arrives, including cases where a word is temporarily ambiguous and later speech may clarify it. It must do so without relying on changes to words it has already committed. Its word error rate should be no more than 5% higher, in relative terms, than that of an equally trained streaming baseline that is allowed to revise its output. At the same time, the 95th-percentile interval from a word’s end to its commitment must be below 800 milliseconds, and committed words must never be revised.
Why specify that the comparison system is both streaming and revisable?

Those terms define what the accuracy comparison is against. It is another streaming recognizer, rather than a system that can wait for the complete speech input before producing output. Unlike the system you want to develop, that baseline may revise words it previously emitted. The goal asks the irreversible-commitment system to stay close to the word error rate of that revisable baseline while meeting its own latency and no-revision requirements.
And what does “equally trained” contribute to that comparison?

It makes the intended comparison one between systems with comparable training, rather than treating a difference in training as part of the target. The goal does not specify a training procedure or a particular baseline result; it specifies the relationship the word error rates should have when compared with an equally trained revisable streaming baseline.
Can you explain the 5% relative requirement without turning it into five percentage points?

Yes. The allowed increase is measured relative to the baseline’s word error rate. For a purely illustrative baseline WER of 10%, a WER within 5% relative would be at most 10.5%, not 15%. The 10% figure is just an example for interpreting the requirement, not a claimed result or a specified baseline value.
So accuracy alone would not establish that the goal was achieved?

Correct. Staying within 5% relative WER of the equally trained revisable streaming baseline addresses the accuracy target, but the goal also requires 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds and zero revisions after commitment. All three conditions matter together.
What exactly starts and ends the latency interval?

For each word, the stated interval starts at the end of that word and ends when the system commits it. It is not measured from the start of the word or from the end of the whole utterance. The goal concerns how long a word remains uncommitted after it has ended.
Does the 800-millisecond threshold mean every word has to be committed that quickly?

No. It applies to the 95th percentile of word-end-to-commit latency, not to the maximum latency of every word. The threshold must be strictly below 800 milliseconds at that percentile. The requirement does not state a separate maximum for the remaining tail of words.
Why is temporary ambiguity central to the goal?

With temporarily ambiguous speech, an early interpretation may be uncertain until more speech arrives. A revisable recognizer can change an earlier output; an irreversible-commitment recognizer cannot change a word once it commits it. The goal is to maintain accurate recognition despite that constraint, while also avoiding excessive delay before commitment.
Does “zero revisions after commitment” mean the system cannot have any uncertainty before committing?

No. It constrains what happens after commitment: a committed word cannot be changed. The goal does not require the system to be certain before every commitment, nor does it specify how uncertainty must be represented beforehand. It does require the final commitment behavior to be irreversible, even when speech was temporarily ambiguous.
Could it wait indefinitely on ambiguous words to protect its WER?

Indefinite waiting would conflict with the latency target if it pushed the 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency to 800 milliseconds or more. The percentile target does not impose an individual deadline on every word, but the recognizer cannot meet the stated goal merely by postponing commitment broadly enough to avoid difficult decisions.
Could it instead commit immediately to satisfy latency?

Speed by itself would not suffice either. Immediate commitment could satisfy the latency aspect while still falling short on accuracy when later speech would have clarified a temporarily ambiguous word. The intended result combines low latency with WER within 5% relative of the equally trained revisable streaming baseline and no changes to committed words.
Is a wrong word that stays unchanged compatible with the no-revision condition?

It is compatible with the no-revision condition considered alone: that condition concerns whether committed output changes, not whether it was correct. A wrong committed word would still affect word error rate, so an approach that preserves errors cannot rely on irreversibility alone to satisfy the full goal.
If a system changes something before labeling it committed, does that automatically violate the requirement?

Not by the wording of this goal. The zero-revision rule begins after commitment. The goal does not prescribe whether any tentative output exists before that point. What matters for the stated finality requirement is that, once a word is committed, it is never revised.
Then commitment has to be meaningful, not just a different name for an output that can still change?

Exactly. In this goal, commitment is the point after which the word is fixed. If a supposedly committed word can subsequently change, it has not met the zero-revisions-after-commitment requirement. The word-end-to-commit latency is measured to that same point of irreversible commitment.
How should I describe the overall challenge in one sentence?

Develop a streaming speech recognizer that resolves temporarily ambiguous speech accurately enough to stay within 5% relative WER of an equally trained revisable streaming baseline, while committing words irreversibly with 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds and zero revisions after commitment.

For the irreversible streaming recognizer, I’m proposing a revision-risk gate trained on streaming hypothesis histories. It would commit buffered words when their calibrated revision risk is below the chosen cutoff, or when they reach a 650-millisecond deadline measured from word end.

That gives each buffered word two routes to commitment: its estimated revision risk falls below the cutoff, or 650 milliseconds have elapsed since the word ended. The first route allows an earlier commitment when the gate indicates sufficiently low risk; the second prevents the policy from waiting beyond its stated deadline simply because the risk has not fallen. Once committed, the word remains fixed under the goal’s zero-revision requirement.
What is the gate meant to learn from a streaming hypothesis history?

The proposed input is the history of hypotheses produced as recognition proceeds, rather than just a single current hypothesis considered in isolation. The gate’s proposed task is to assess the risk of committing a buffered word while its interpretation might still change. The proposal does not specify the gate’s model, its exact input representation, or how it is trained beyond using streaming hypothesis histories.
Does “revision risk” mean the same thing as whether a word is definitely correct?

Not necessarily. Here it is a risk measure for deciding whether to commit a buffered word that might otherwise be revised. It is useful for the commitment decision, but the proposal does not assert that a low-risk estimate guarantees correctness. Accuracy still matters independently: a committed error cannot be repaired afterward.
What is the role of calibration in that rule?

Calibration is part of the proposed gate: the decision is based on calibrated risk, so the cutoff is meant to be applied to a risk estimate with a meaningful interpretation. The node does not specify a calibration procedure, a numerical cutoff, or a demonstrated level of calibration. Those are not results established by the proposal.
So the 650 milliseconds is the cutoff for risk?

No. The two cutoffs concern different things. The risk cutoff governs whether a buffered word can be committed before the deadline; its numerical value is not given. The 650-millisecond value is a time deadline measured from the word’s end. Reaching that deadline is itself a reason to commit, even if the risk has not dropped below the chosen cutoff.
What if the speech is still ambiguous at the 650-millisecond mark?

Under the proposed rule, the deadline still triggers commitment. That is where the tension between latency and accuracy is clearest: waiting longer might help with an ambiguous word, but this policy calls for committing at the 650-millisecond word-end deadline if the lower-risk route has not triggered first. The proposal does not claim that every such decision will be correct.
And if the risk drops below the cutoff well before then?

The policy would commit the buffered word at that earlier point. It does not require waiting for the deadline once the calibrated risk satisfies the early-commit condition. The deadline is the fallback for words that have not qualified for earlier commitment.
Why buffer the words at all instead of treating each provisional hypothesis as a commitment?

Buffering separates a word under consideration from a word that has been irreversibly committed. That distinction lets the proposed gate use the streaming hypothesis history to decide when to make a buffered word final. Treating every provisional hypothesis as final would remove that opportunity, while allowing changes after commitment would conflict with the zero-revision goal.
Is the 650-millisecond deadline the same as the goal’s latency threshold?

No. The proposed policy uses a 650-millisecond deadline for committing a buffered word after its end. The goal sets a separate performance requirement: 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds. The policy’s deadline is part of a proposed approach, not a reported measurement showing that the percentile requirement has been met.
Would it be fair to say this proposal already meets the word error rate target because it uses calibrated risk?

No. A calibrated revision-risk gate is a proposed way to decide when to commit; it is not evidence of achieved recognition accuracy. The word error rate would still need to be within 5% relative of an equally trained revisable streaming baseline. The proposal supplies neither a measured WER nor a comparison result.
Could the gate simply refuse to commit a high-risk word after the deadline?

That would not follow the rule as proposed. The rule says to commit buffered words when risk is below the cutoff *or* at the 650-millisecond word-end deadline. The deadline is not conditional on the risk becoming low. There may be a difficult tradeoff for high-risk words at that point, but this proposal does not include a further exception.
Is the deadline measured from when the gate first sees the word?

It is specified as a word-end deadline: 650 milliseconds from the word’s end, not from the moment the gate first considers or buffers it. That matches the kind of interval used in the goal’s word-end-to-commit latency requirement, while remaining a distinct, proposed policy value.
Can I describe this as training the recognizer itself to revise less often?

That would change the proposal. What is stated is to train a *revision-risk gate* on streaming hypothesis histories and use it to govern commitment of buffered words. The proposal does not say that the recognizer itself is retrained to revise less often, nor does it report a reduction in revisions of provisional hypotheses.
Then the central idea is to use the history to decide when uncertainty has eased enough to commit, but still have a firm time limit?

Yes, with one important qualification: the gate uses streaming hypothesis histories to estimate *calibrated revision risk*, and early commitment occurs when that risk is below the cutoff. If it does not cross the cutoff, the buffered word is committed at the 650-millisecond word-end deadline. This describes the proposed decision rule, not a finding that the accuracy and latency targets have already been achieved.
What fraction of temporarily ambiguous words remain high-risk at the 650-ms forced-commit deadline?

That fraction is not given. The question asks how often a temporarily ambiguous word reaches 650 milliseconds after its end without its revision risk having fallen enough for an earlier commitment. The proposed gate and deadline define the situation, but they do not tell us how many words fall into it.
What would the fraction be a fraction of?

As phrased, the denominator is the temporarily ambiguous words under consideration. The numerator is the subset that remain high-risk when the 650-millisecond word-end deadline arrives. That differs from asking what fraction of *all* words reach the deadline, or what fraction of words still buffered at the deadline are high-risk.
Does reaching the deadline automatically mean a word is high-risk?

Under the proposed rule, a buffered word that qualified as below the calibrated-risk cutoff would have been committed earlier. So a word still awaiting the forced-commit deadline has not satisfied that early-commit condition. Whether to call that state “high-risk” depends on how the question uses the term; no separate numerical definition of high-risk is supplied.
Would a temporarily ambiguous word committed before 650 milliseconds count in the numerator?

No, not if the numerator means words that *remain* high-risk at the forced-commit deadline. A word committed earlier because its risk fell below the cutoff would not be waiting for forced commitment then. It can still belong to the overall group of temporarily ambiguous words used as the denominator.
Is the question about risk exactly 650 milliseconds after each word ends, rather than 650 milliseconds after it first appears in a hypothesis?

Yes. The deadline in the proposal is measured from word end. The question concerns the risk state at that word-end deadline, not after a fixed interval from the first hypothesis or the first time the gate considers the word.
If I knew how often the gate commits words early, would that answer it?

Not necessarily. An overall early-commit fraction could include words that were never temporarily ambiguous. This question is specifically about the temporarily ambiguous subset and asks how many of those still present high risk at the 650-millisecond forced-commit point.
Could I infer the fraction from the fact that the deadline is 650 milliseconds?

No. The deadline tells us *when* a forced commitment occurs, not how often risk remains high at that time. That frequency depends on how the risk evolves for the temporarily ambiguous words in question; no such distribution or count has been provided.
What if some ambiguous words remain difficult even after the deadline?

They would still be subject to the proposed forced-commit rule at 650 milliseconds after word end. Their possible difficulty afterward does not supply the fraction asked for: the question is specifically how many temporarily ambiguous words are still high-risk *at* the deadline.
Does this question ask what proportion of forced commitments turn out to be wrong?

No. Remaining high-risk at the deadline concerns the gate’s assessment at commitment time. Being wrong concerns the eventual recognition outcome. Those quantities may be relevant to each other, but the question does not equate them, and it provides no error rate for forced commitments.
Why single out temporarily ambiguous words rather than asking about every word?

Because the question focuses on the cases where the recognizer may initially lack enough context for a stable interpretation. For those words, it is especially pertinent whether the risk falls before the 650-millisecond deadline or remains high when the policy forces a commitment. The wording does not ask for a population-wide rate across unambiguous and ambiguous words combined.
Could the answer be expressed as a percentage?

Yes, once the relevant fraction is known. It would be the number of temporarily ambiguous words that remain high-risk at the 650-millisecond word-end deadline divided by the number of temporarily ambiguous words being considered, multiplied by 100. No counts are supplied, so assigning a numerical percentage would be unsupported.
Would you answer differently if someone asked for the fraction among words that actually reach forced commitment?

Yes. That conditions on reaching forced commitment and uses a narrower denominator. Your question instead names temporarily ambiguous words as the group of interest, including ones whose risk may drop enough for early commitment. The two fractions should not be treated as interchangeable.
So what can we say confidently about the answer right now?

We can state precisely what is being asked: among temporarily ambiguous words, what share still have high revision risk at the forced-commit point 650 milliseconds after word end? We cannot state the share itself from the information given.
Here is a hypothesis for the deadline question: on ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words, fewer than 8% exceed 10% calibrated revision risk at the 650-ms deadline.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis, not an observed fraction. It says that among ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words, the share with calibrated revision risk strictly greater than 10% at the deadline 650 milliseconds after word end is strictly less than 8%. It gives the earlier question a defined group of words and a numerical meaning for “high-risk.”
What is the denominator in that statement?

The denominator is the ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words covered by the hypothesis. The numerator is those words whose calibrated revision risk exceeds 10% at the 650-ms deadline. It is not a percentage of all StreamMix words or a percentage of only the words that undergo forced commitment.
Does “fewer than 8%” allow exactly 8%?

No. It is a strict inequality: the proposed fraction is less than 8%, not less than or equal to 8%. Likewise, “exceed 10%” means risk strictly greater than 10%; a risk of exactly 10% does not count in that numerator.
So is the hypothesis saying that every ambiguity-tagged word has low risk by then?

No. It allows some ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words to exceed 10% calibrated revision risk at the deadline, but hypothesizes that they account for fewer than 8% of the group. If risks are available for the full group at that point, the complementary statement is that more than 92% are at or below 10% risk. Neither statement says the high-risk group is empty.
Are the 8% and 10% figures measuring the same thing?

No. The 10% figure is a threshold applied to each word’s calibrated revision risk. The 8% figure concerns the fraction of ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words whose risk exceeds that threshold at the deadline. One is a risk level; the other is a share of words.
Is 10% necessarily the gate’s early-commit cutoff?

The hypothesis does not say that. It uses 10% to define which words count as exceeding the risk level at the deadline. The proposed gate commits buffered words when their calibrated risk falls below a chosen cutoff, but no numerical value for that early-commit cutoff has been specified. We should not equate the two thresholds without that additional condition.
And this is still the same 650-ms deadline measured from each word’s end?

Yes. The hypothesis refers to the proposed forced-commit deadline, 650 milliseconds after word end. It does not measure 650 milliseconds from the start of a word, the first hypothesis containing it, or the end of the utterance.
How does this relate to my question about temporarily ambiguous words?

It offers a more specifically framed hypothesis relevant to that question: it concerns *ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words* and defines the risk condition as exceeding 10% calibrated revision risk at the 650-ms deadline. It does not establish that the same fraction applies to every possible set of temporarily ambiguous words outside that named group.
Could I treat this as the measured answer for StreamMix?
No. The statement is a hypothesis that the fraction is below 8%, not a report that it has been measured. It supplies a proposed numerical answer to assess, but no counts or results are provided here.
Does it imply that fewer than 8% of those words would actually be revised if revision were allowed?

Not directly. The hypothesis is about calibrated *revision risk* exceeding 10% at a particular time, not an observed revision rate. It separates words by an estimated risk threshold; it does not report how many would actually be revised.
Nor does it mean fewer than 8% would be recognized incorrectly?

Right. The fraction exceeding the revision-risk threshold is not a word error rate. A risk estimate, an actual revision, and a recognition error are different quantities. This hypothesis alone does not give an error rate for ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words or for the recognizer overall.
Does the word “calibrated” turn the hypothesis into a certainty about individual words?

No. It describes the kind of revision-risk estimate used in the hypothesis. It does not make an individual word’s outcome certain, and it does not establish that calibration has been achieved. The hypothesis remains a claim about the distribution of those risk estimates at the deadline.
What about words the gate commits before the deadline—are they automatically outside this hypothesis?

The hypothesis names ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words as its group, not merely words still buffered for forced commitment. Its wording does not spell out how a word committed early would be assigned a risk value *at* the deadline. That detail would need to be handled consistently when interpreting the fraction; we should not silently change the denominator to only deadline-forced words.
If the hypothesis held, would it show that the overall recognition goal was met?

No. It would address this particular risk-at-deadline question for ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words. The broader goal separately requires word error rate within 5% relative of an equally trained revisable streaming baseline, 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds, and zero revisions after commitment. The risk-fraction hypothesis does not itself establish those outcomes.
Can you restate the hypothesis without accidentally making it sound like a result?

We hypothesize that, among ambiguity-tagged StreamMix words, fewer than 8% have calibrated revision risk greater than 10% at the forced-commit deadline 650 milliseconds after word end. That states the proposed bound while leaving open whether the fraction actually satisfies it.

To evaluate the risk-at-deadline hypothesis, let’s calibrate revision risk on StreamMix-dev, replay ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test, and count words exceeding 10% risk at the 650-ms word-end deadline.

That activity separates calibration from the deadline count. Revision risk is calibrated on StreamMix-dev. Then ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test is replayed, and the count of words whose calibrated revision risk is strictly greater than 10% is taken at 650 milliseconds after each word ends. The activity describes what to do; it does not yet give a count or a conclusion about the hypothesis.
Why name both StreamMix-dev and StreamMix-test?

They have different roles in the stated activity. StreamMix-dev is where revision risk is calibrated; ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test is what gets replayed and counted. The instruction does not say to calibrate on StreamMix-test or to obtain the deadline count from StreamMix-dev.
When you say “replay,” is the point to consider the streaming hypotheses as they unfold?

Yes, that is the natural reading in this streaming-recognition context: examine the ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words as the streaming process reaches the relevant time for each word. The activity does not prescribe a particular replay implementation or specify additional measurements during replay.
What precisely should be counted?

Count ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words whose calibrated revision risk exceeds 10% at the 650-ms word-end deadline. “Exceeds” is strict: a word assessed at exactly 10% risk would not be included in that count. The instruction is about words, not utterances or individual hypothesis updates.
Does 650 ms run from when the word first appears in a hypothesis?

No. It is a word-end deadline. The relevant time is 650 milliseconds after that word ends, regardless of when it first appeared in a streaming hypothesis. Using another starting point would answer a different timing question.
Does this activity require counting words whose risk crossed 10% at any earlier point?
No. The specified count concerns risk *at* the 650-ms word-end deadline. A word’s risk at some earlier instant, or its highest risk over the replay, is not the quantity named here.
If I only report that count, can I compare it with the fewer-than-8% hypothesis?

A count alone does not express a fraction. For that comparison, the count would need to be considered relative to the ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words in the group being assessed. The stated activity explicitly calls for counting words over 10% risk; it provides neither the count nor the resulting fraction.
Are the 10% and 8% numbers doing different jobs again?

Yes. In this activity, 10% is the calibrated revision-risk threshold applied to each word at the deadline. The related hypothesis asks whether the share of ambiguity-tagged words exceeding that threshold is fewer than 8%. The activity does not state an observed share.
Do I count only words that the gate was forced to commit at the deadline?

The activity says to replay *ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test* and count words exceeding 10% risk at the deadline; it does not explicitly restrict the group to words forced to commit. If a word was committed earlier, the wording does not specify how its risk at the later deadline is represented. That point needs a consistent interpretation before treating a deadline count as a fraction of all ambiguity-tagged words. It would not be faithful to silently replace the stated group with forced-commit words only.
Could we treat an early commitment as automatically having no risk at 650 ms?

The activity does not establish that convention. An early commitment and a risk estimate at the 650-ms point are distinct notions. Assigning an automatic value to early-committed words would add a rule not specified here, so it should not be presented as part of the activity.
Does calibrating revision risk on StreamMix-dev by itself say that the estimates are accurate on StreamMix-test?

No. It states where calibration is to occur, not a measured result on StreamMix-test. The subsequent replay and count concern the specified test words, but this activity gives no outcome for them and no claim about how well calibration transfers.
Is the deadline count a count of actual revisions?

No. It counts words whose *calibrated revision-risk estimate* exceeds 10% at the specified time. It does not count observed revisions, nor does it directly count recognition errors. Those would be different quantities.
And we are not changing the gate’s early-commit cutoff to 10% just because this activity uses that threshold?

Correct. The 10% value defines what this deadline count includes. The proposal describes early commitment below a calibrated-risk cutoff but does not specify that cutoff numerically. The activity does not equate it with 10% or change the commitment rule.
Would this activity also establish the word error rate and latency goals?

Not on its own. It is directed at the fraction of ambiguity-tagged words above a specified risk level at the 650-ms deadline. The broader goal also involves WER relative to an equally trained revisable streaming baseline, 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds, and zero revisions after commitment. This activity does not supply those measurements or establish that they meet their requirements.
So what is the most precise way to state what we’re doing without implying that we already know the outcome?

Calibrate revision risk on StreamMix-dev; replay ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test; and, for the words under assessment, count those with calibrated revision risk strictly above 10% at the deadline 650 milliseconds after word end. That describes the planned activity without claiming a count, a fraction, or confirmation of the hypothesis.
The replay result is in: on ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test, 6.4% of words exceeded 10% calibrated revision risk at the 650-ms word-end deadline.

That is the observed risk-at-deadline fraction for the named group. Among ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words, 6.4% had calibrated revision risk strictly greater than 10% at the point 650 milliseconds after word end. It is a share of words, not the average revision risk of those words.
Can you separate the two percentages for me?

The 10% is the risk threshold applied to each word. The 6.4% is the fraction of ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words whose calibrated revision risk exceeded that threshold at the deadline. They describe different quantities.
Would a word assessed at exactly 10% risk be included in the 6.4%?
No. “Exceeded 10%” means strictly greater than 10%. A word at exactly 10% risk is not in the reported 6.4%.
What does the rest of the group represent?
The remaining 93.6% did not exceed 10% calibrated revision risk at the specified point. That does not, by itself, say when those words were committed or whether their recognition was correct.
Is this a result for all StreamMix-test words?
No. The reported group is ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words. Extending the 6.4% figure to all StreamMix-test words, or to other speech, would go beyond this result.
And the time point is 650 ms after each word ends?
Yes. The assessment is at the 650-millisecond word-end deadline for each word—not 650 milliseconds after its first appearance in a hypothesis or after the utterance ends.
Can I call 6.4% the forced-commit rate?

Not from this evidence alone. It is the fraction exceeding the specified calibrated-risk threshold at the deadline. The result does not state what fraction of words were actually committed by the deadline rule rather than earlier, and it does not identify the risk threshold used for early commitment.
Does it tell us that 6.4% of the words would actually have been revised?

No. Exceeding 10% *estimated revision risk* is not the same as undergoing a revision. The 6.4% figure reports how many words fell above a risk threshold at that time; it is not an observed revision frequency.
Could I interpret it as a word error rate for ambiguous words?
No. The result does not report which recognized words were correct or incorrect. A calibrated revision-risk threshold and word error rate are different measures, so 6.4% should not be labeled a WER.
What about the number of words behind that percentage?
The evidence gives the percentage but not the underlying count or the total number of ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test words. We should not infer either count from 6.4% alone.
What is a concise statement I can use without implying more than we observed?

On ambiguity-tagged StreamMix-test, 6.4% of words had calibrated revision risk greater than 10% at the deadline 650 milliseconds after word end. This reports a risk-threshold fraction at a specified time, not an error rate or an actual revision rate.
I’ve decided to retain the 650-ms forced-commit deadline for prototyping because only 6.4% of ambiguity-tagged words exceed 10% revision risk at that deadline.

That keeps the proposed deadline in place for prototyping. The reason is the observed 6.4% figure: among the ambiguity-tagged words assessed, that share exceeded 10% revision risk at the deadline. The decision is to retain the 650-millisecond forced-commit point, not to claim that the recognizer has met its overall accuracy or latency goals.
What does “retain” mean here?

It means continuing to use the 650-ms forced-commit deadline in the prototype rather than changing that deadline as part of this decision. It does not say the deadline is permanent or establish a result for a finished recognizer.
And the deadline is still measured from word end?

Yes. A buffered word reaches the forced-commit deadline 650 milliseconds after that word ends. The decision keeps that timing rule; it does not redefine the interval as beginning when the word first appears in a hypothesis.
How does the 6.4% figure justify keeping the deadline?

It is the stated reason for the prototyping decision: at the deadline, only 6.4% of the ambiguity-tagged words exceeded the specified 10% revision-risk level. That gives the decision a concrete risk-at-deadline observation. It does not mean that the remaining words are guaranteed correct or that forcing commitment carries no risk.
Is 6.4% the revision risk of each of those words?

No. It is a fraction of words. Each word is assessed against a revision-risk threshold of 10%, and 6.4% of the ambiguity-tagged words exceed that threshold at the 650-ms deadline. The statement does not give the individual risk values of those words.
Does this decision make 10% the gate’s early-commit cutoff?

No. The 10% figure describes the risk level used in the observation supporting the decision. The proposed gate commits buffered words early when calibrated risk is below a chosen cutoff, but this decision does not specify that cutoff or equate it with 10%.
What happens under the retained rule if a buffered word still has high revision risk at 650 ms?

The forced-commit deadline still applies: the buffered word is committed at 650 milliseconds after word end if it has not been committed earlier. The decision retains that rule despite the fact that some ambiguity-tagged words exceed 10% revision risk at that point. Once a word is committed, the goal calls for no revisions to it.
Could I say the 6.4% are the words that will be wrong when forced to commit?

No. The figure identifies words above a revision-risk threshold at the deadline, not words known to be recognized incorrectly. The decision uses that risk observation as its reason; it does not turn the observation into an error count.
Could I call it the percentage of words forced to commit?

Not on the stated evidence. The 6.4% is the share exceeding 10% revision risk at the deadline. The percentage actually committed through the deadline route, rather than through the earlier low-risk route, is not specified by this decision.
Does retaining 650 ms mean the 95th-percentile latency is already below 800 ms?

The decision does not report a measured 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency. It retains a 650-ms word-end deadline for prototyping, while the broader goal calls for a 95th-percentile latency below 800 milliseconds. The decision should not be presented as a measurement establishing that goal.
What about the word error rate comparison with the revisable baseline?

This decision does not report word error rate for either system. The broader accuracy requirement remains WER within 5% relative of an equally trained revisable streaming baseline, but the 6.4% risk-threshold fraction is not that comparison.
So what is the exact scope of the decision?

Retain the 650-ms word-end forced-commit deadline for prototyping, for the stated reason that only 6.4% of the ambiguity-tagged words assessed exceed 10% revision risk at that deadline. It is a decision about the prototype’s commitment timing, not a declaration that every ambiguous word is safe to commit or that all performance requirements have been demonstrated.
I want to phrase it without overstating the result.

“Retain the 650-ms word-end forced-commit deadline for prototyping, because 6.4% of ambiguity-tagged words exceeded 10% revision risk at that deadline.” That preserves both the decision and its reason without describing the risk fraction as an error rate or a final performance result.

The next plan is to implement 650-ms risk-gated commits, then test on StreamMix-test whether WER is within 5% relative of an equally-trained revisable streaming baseline, p95 word-end-to-commit latency is below 800 ms, and there are zero revisions after commitment.

That is an implementation and evaluation plan, not a report of completed performance. The recognizer would use risk-gated commitments with a 650-millisecond word-end forced-commit deadline. The StreamMix-test evaluation would then check the three stated outcomes: the relative WER comparison, 95th-percentile word-end-to-commit latency below 800 milliseconds, and no revisions to committed words.
Does “risk-gated” mean every word must wait until 650 ms?

No. Under the proposed rule, a buffered word can be committed earlier when its calibrated revision risk falls below the chosen cutoff. The 650-ms point is the forced-commit deadline measured from word end, not the required waiting time for every word.
If the risk has not fallen below the cutoff when the deadline arrives, what does the plan call for?

The retained rule calls for commitment at the 650-ms word-end deadline. Risk can permit earlier commitment, but it does not postpone commitment beyond that deadline under this plan. A committed word must then remain unchanged.
Is the risk cutoff specified as 10% in this implementation plan?

No numerical early-commit risk cutoff is specified here. The plan says to implement risk-gated commits with the 650-ms deadline. It should not be read as assigning a particular value to the gate’s cutoff.
What exactly are we comparing for the WER test?
